extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political philosophy, legislators, and constitutional designers
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria for assessing and constructing forms of government (monarchy, aristocracy, oligarchy, democracy, mixed states, tyranny), including institutional arrangements for assemblies, magistracies, courts, military composition, and the role of the middle class. Focuses on practical prescriptions for stability and justice applicable to city-states or polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of the law vs. men
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme power of a well-constituted state should reside in the law rather than in particular men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good constitution not only makes good laws but enforces obedience to them; enforcement is evidence of a well-constituted state. When offices and power concentrate in particular men (e.g., rich oligarchs or demagogues) rather than in the law, the constitution is degraded. Examples: in some oligarchies the supreme power is lodged in the laws when many with moderate property govern; when the few rich dominate, power shifts to men rather than laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of regimes (types and species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments are classified into monarchy, oligarchy, democracy, aristocracy (properly so called), a mixed 'state' (polity), and tyranny; many of these have internal species determined by property distribution and institutional rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and name the form correctly because diagnosis and remedies depend on the particular type (e.g., several species of democracies and oligarchies arise from differences in wealth distribution, selection of magistrates, and practices like fines/pay for attendance). Plato’s fourfold enumeration is not exhaustive; mixtures and rare types exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy properly defined (rule of the best by virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy properly so-called is government by the best men upon the most virtuous principles—where men are both good persons and good citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial uses of 'aristocracy' to mean simply rule by the rich or the virtuous should be distinguished; only a polity in which virtue is the public concern and the rulers aim at the common good deserves the name. Variants: governments that favor rich+virtuous+citizens (e.g., Carthage) are 'a sort of aristocracy'; Lacedaemon is a 'virtuous democracy' when virtue and broad citizenship are combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government (free state/polity) should blend oligarchy and democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A free state (polity) is a mixture of oligarchy and democracy; it should take parts of each to form a stable medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three methods to blend: (1) adopt rules from each for corresponding departments (e.g., judicial rules), (2) take a middle measure between opposing practices (e.g., intermediate census), (3) adopt different laws from each for different offices (e.g., choose magistrates by vote as oligarchies do, but admit broad participation as democracies do). The best proof of a happy mixture is when the same state may properly be called both a democracy and an oligarchy; stability must be secured from within (citizen commitment), not foreign forbearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the middle class (middle state) for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A political community is most perfect and stable when the middle class (those of moderate and convenient fortune) is numerous and predominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Middle-status citizens are less likely to be extreme in vice or to breed sedition; they make good rulers and are best disposed to obey and command in turn. Legislators should frame constitutions to favor and enlarge the middle rank because too many rich or poor lead to oligarchy, democracy, or tyranny. Historical lawgivers (Solon, Lycurgus) often came from the middle rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding regime change: maintain sufficient middle class to prevent takeover
rubrics_metrics.description: Regime change to democracy or oligarchy (and thence possibly to tyranny) commonly follows when the number of middle-class citizens is too small relative to rich or poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instability arises when one extreme overbalances the middle; conquerors often impose the form of government that suits their own class interests rather than what is best for the state. Therefore constitutions should aim to preserve or create a sizeable middle to prevent factional domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property distribution determines species of oligarchy/democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and species of oligarchy or democracy depend on the distribution of property and who has leisure/ability to manage public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (a) Oligarchy when most have moderate property and laws govern (law supremacy); (b) Oligarchy of the second sort when few have large property and associate to rule; (c) Oligarchy of the third sort when offices become hereditary and then may evolve into monarchy. Democracies vary when city enlargement and public revenue allow poor citizens leisure (paid attendance), placing supreme power with the poor. Institutional details (pay, fines, census) determine the practical species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three institutional pillars legislators must consider
rubrics_metrics.description: A careful legislator must consider (1) the public assembly, (2) the officers (who they are, powers, appointment), and (3) the judicial department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three determine most of what makes states differ and what makes them successful. Any constitutional design must specify the scope of the assembly, the structure and selection of magistrates, and the composition and incentives of courts to suit the desired regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper functions of the public assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: The public assembly should determine war and peace, make/break alliances, enact laws, sentence to death/banishment/confiscation, and call magistrates to account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which of these powers belong to all citizens, some magistrates, or a mix, recognizing trade-offs between broad participation and efficient/informed decision-making. The assembly works best when its powers are sensibly delegated for day-to-day business but retained for major acts and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of delegating deliberative power (vote vs lot; rotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are multiple legitimate methods of vesting deliberative power: (a) rotation so citizens execute powers by turn; (b) a supreme council of magistrates divided by tribes/wards for phased service; (c) people meet only for certain large tasks while magistrates manage daily business; (d) pure democracy where all deliberate on all matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different regimes will choose different mixes: oligarchies favor restricted deliberative bodies, democracies favor frequent assemblies. Combining selection by lot and by vote, or alternating methods, can secure balance. Where councils are used, include equal representation of ranks when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives for attendance and participation (fines and pay)
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure genuine participation, legislatures should use fines and payments: fine non-attending persons and/or pay poorer citizens for attendance so assemblies and courts are representative and cannot be subverted by class differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oligarchies often fine rich but excuse poor; democracies often pay the poor but expect rich to attend unpaid. Best practice in a mixed/polity is to extend both pay and fine to every member or to calibrate them so that attendance produces a balanced representation (e.g., pay enough poor to equalize numbers or use lot to limit numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship should be tied to bearing arms
rubrics_metrics.description: The political community ought ideally to consist of those who bear arms (or have borne them), making land/military service a basis of civic standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Census or enrollment should be sufficiently extensive so that those enrolled constitute more of the people than those not. Historical forms varied: some states included only veterans or those who had borne arms, while larger states expanded citizenship as reliance on foot troops increased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition rules: quantity vs quality must be balanced
rubrics_metrics.description: Every city consists of qualitative attributes (liberty, riches, education, family) and quantity (populousness); the constitution must properly adjust quantity to quality so that number does not overturn the value of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If numbers of a class (e.g., poor, husbandmen, mechanics) exceed proportionate influence, the state will take that form (democracy of husbandmen, democracy of mechanics). Legislators should tune laws to favor the intended dominant balance, especially to secure the middle class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mixed procedures in magistrate selection (votes and lots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining election by vote for some offices and selection by lot for others (or mixing both) helps blend aristocratic and democratic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choose some magistrates by vote as oligarchies do, and use lot or broad admission as democracies do for other positions. When councils are to include both ranks, elect an equal number of citizens and nobles by vote or lot to maintain balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and design of magistracies (term, eligibility, duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing magistracies consider how many there shall be, precise offices, term lengths (months, years, perpetual), reappointment rules, eligibility, method of appointment, and whether offices should be held by the same person multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In large states prefer single-purpose offices (one employment per person) because focused attention yields better outcomes; in small states combine offices since manpower is limited. Technical roles should be filled by persons skilled in those matters; avoid hereditary succession that entrenches oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial department design and attendance enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Court composition and enforcement differ by regime: oligarchies may fine the rich for non-attendance, democracies may pay the poor for attendance; different eligibility rules determine who sits in judgment of capital causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is to blend systems, copy oligarchic enforcement in courts and democratic inclusiveness in assemblies (reward poor for attendance), or create pre-advisers/guardians of the laws to propose measures before the people vote, thereby giving the populace a role without enabling disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-limiting of popular initiative and punishment powers
rubrics_metrics.description: In mixed regimes, it may be prudent to grant the populace the power to vote on proposed bills but not to initiate proposals contrary to magistrates, or to allow advice without decisive authority; similarly, the people may be given power of pardoning but not of condemning (or vice versa depending on the regime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limits prevent unskilled masses or factional majorities from destabilizing the constitution while preserving a channel for popular oversight. For instance, allow the people to vote on measures proposed by magistrates, or have them hear causes but refer condemnations to magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy/oligarchy/democracy objective differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Each regime prizes a different good: aristocracy seeks virtue, oligarchy seeks riches, democracy seeks liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and institutional choices should reflect which good is being promoted; recognizing these aims explains many legal/administrative choices (e.g., fines, pay, office eligibility) and helps diagnose when a regime is drifting toward a deformed variant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and species of tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny is rule by one for his own advantage, not the advantage of the governed; it rules by compulsion and is the opposite of kingly power (which may be regulated by law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tyrannies can resemble monarchies in form but differ in accountability and purpose. Tyranny often arises from excesses of democracy or oligarchy; check for rulers who govern without being answerable or who aim at private gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation criterion: internal foundations of constitution stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-composed state should preserve itself by making every member unwilling to alter the constitution; its means of preservation should be internal, not dependent on neighbors' forbearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability arises from broad acceptance—if all parts of the constitution secure the interests of major groups (especially the middle), citizens will resist change. External peace or a ruler's personal power is not a lasting foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military composition affects political form
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization and social basis of the military (horse, heavy-armed foot, militia, veterans) influence who governs and how widely political rights attach to the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early reliance on cavalry (horse) concentrated power in fewer hands; later reliance on large foot forces expanded the number of citizens with a stake in the constitution. Legislators should consider who bears arms when determining enrollment and political rights.
